# Exercise 1. 
Calculate the standard deviations for
• all distributions in Exercise 5, Week 2;
• the profit in both cases in Exercise 8, Week 2.

## Solution
### Standard deviations for Exercise 5, Week 2

\begin{align*}
E(X) &= \sum x_i p_i \\
\text{Var}(X) &= E(X - E(X))^2 = \sum (x_i - E(X))^2 p_i \\
\text{Var}(X) &= E(X^2) - (E(X))^2 = \sum x_i^2 p_i - (E(X))^2 \\
\sigma &= \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}
\end{align*}

```{r}
num.simulations <- 1e6
my.sd <- function(x,p){
  # using the formula Var(X) = E(X^2) - (EX)^2
  cat(paste0("Theoretical value: ",sqrt(sum(x^2*p) - sum(x*p)^2),"\n"))
  cat(paste0("Simulated value: ",sd(sample(x,num.simulations,replace=TRUE,prob=p)),"\n"))
}
```

1. 

```{r}
x<-c(0,1,2,3)
p<-c(0.125,0.375,0.375,0.125)

E_X <- sum(x*p)
Var_X <- sum((x-E_X)^2*p)
sd_X <- sqrt(Var_X) 
sd_X   
my.sd(x,p)
```

2. 

```{r}
x<-c(20,25,30,35)
p<-c(0.2,0.15,0.25,0.4)

E_X <- sum(x*p)
Var_X <- sum((x-E_X)^2*p)
sd_X <- sqrt(Var_X) 
sd_X   
my.sd(x,p) 
```

3. 

```{r}
x<-c(0,1,2,3,4,5)
p<-c(0.18,0.39,0.24,0.14,0.04,0.01)
E_X <- sum(x*p)
Var_X <- sum((x-E_X)^2*p)
sd_X <- sqrt(Var_X) 
sd_X
```

4. 

```{r}

p<-c(0.1,0.2,0.3,0.25,0.1,0.05)
E_X <- sum(x*p)
Var_X <- sum((x-E_X)^2*p)
sd_X <- sqrt(Var_X)
```

### The profit in both cases in Exercise 8, Week 2

A reminder of the problem...

> A company is contracted to finish a e100 000 project by 31 December. If
the company does not complete the project on time, a penalty of e8000 per month (or
part of a month) is incurred. The company estimates that if it continues alone there will
be a 40% chance of completing on time and that the project may be one, two, three or
four months late with equal probability.
Subcontractors can be hired by the firm at a cost of e18 000. If the subcontractors
are hired then the probability that the company completes on time is doubled. If the
project is still late it will now be only one or two months late with equal probability.
State which option is better for the company after determining the expected profit when
(i) subcontractors are not used;
(ii) subcontractors are used.

#### Subcontractors are not used
```{r}
x<-c(100000, 92000, 84000, 76000, 68000)
p<-c(0.4, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15)
E_X <- sum(x*p)
Var_X <- sum((x-E_X)^2*p)
sd_X <- sqrt(Var_X)
cat(paste0("Expected profit: ",E_X,"\n"))
cat(paste0("Standard deviation: ",sd_X,"\n"))
```

#### Subcontractors are used
```{r}
x<-c(100000, 92000, 84000)
p<-c(0.4, 0.3, 0.3)
x <- x - 18000 # subtract the cost of subcontractors

E_X <- sum(x*p)
Var_X <- sum((x-E_X)^2*p)
sd_X <- sqrt(Var_X)
cat(paste0("Expected profit: ",E_X,"\n"))
cat(paste0("Standard deviation: ",sd_X,"\n"))
```

The expected profit is higher when subcontractors are not used, but the 
standard deviation is lower when subcontractors are used. The company should 
consider its risk tolerance when making a decision.

# Exercise 2. 
Calculate the expectation and the standard deviation for:
• the number of invoices paid within 10 days in Exercise 10, Week 2;
• the number of selected people in Exercise 11, Week 2;
• the number of ex-smokers in the sample in Exercise 12, Week 2;
• the number of children with a high blood lead level in each of the three situations
of Exercise 14, Week 2;

## Solution
### The number of invoices paid within 10 days in Exercise 10, Week 2

> A firm offers a 1% early-payment discount if an invoice is paid within 10
days and the full amount is due after 10 days. In the past, 30% of all invoices have been
paid within 10 days. If the firm sends out 8 invoices during the first week of January...

```{r}
n <- 8
p <- 0.3
E_X <- n*p
Var_X <- n*p*(1-p)
sd_X <- sqrt(Var_X)
cat(paste0("Expected number of invoices paid within 10 days: ",E_X,"\n"))
cat(paste0("Standard deviation: ",sd_X,"\n"))
```

### The number of selected people in Exercise 11, Week 2

> Each of 2208 people has a 5% chance to be selected, independently of each
other. Find the probability that the number of selected people will be
(i) exactly 110; (ii) greater than 120; (iii) less than 100; (iv) between 90 and 110.

1. X = 110

```{r}
n <- 2208
p <- 0.05
E_X <- n*p
Var_X <- n*p*(1-p)
sd_X <- sqrt(Var_X)

# Calculate the probability using the normal approximation
x <- 110
z <- (x - E_X) / sd_X
p <- pnorm(z)
cat(paste0("Probability of exactly 110 selected people: ",p,"\n"))
```

2. X > 120

```{r}
x <- 120
z <- (x - E_X) / sd_X
p <- 1 - pnorm(z)
cat(paste0("Probability of more than 120 selected people: ",p,"\n"))
```

3. X < 100

```{r}
x <- 100
z <- (x - E_X) / sd_X
p <- pnorm(z)
cat(paste0("Probability of less than 100 selected people: ",p,"\n"))
```

4. 90 < X < 110

```{r}
x1 <- 90
x2 <- 110
z1 <- (x1 - E_X) / sd_X
z2 <- (x2 - E_X) / sd_X
p <- pnorm(z2) - pnorm(z1)
cat(paste0("Probability of between 90 and 110 selected people: ",p,"\n"))
```

### The number of ex-smokers in the sample in Exercise 12, Week 2

> In 2015, ex-smokers constituted 34.0% of all adults in the UK. For a survey,
a sample of 1 500 people was selected selected uniformly at random from all adults in the
UK. Calculate the probabilities that the number of ex-smokers in the sample will be
(i) exactly 510; (ii) between 500 and 520 inclusive; (iii) between 470 and 550 inclusive.

1. X = 510

```{r}
n <- 1500
p <- 0.34
E_X <- n*p
Var_X <- n*p*(1-p)
sd_X <- sqrt(Var_X)

cat(paste0("Expected number of ex-smokers: ",E_X,"\n"))
cat(paste0("Standard deviation: ",sd_X,"\n"))
```

```{r}
# Calculate the probability using the normal approximation
x <- 510
z <- (x - E_X) / sd_X
p <- pnorm(z)
cat(paste0("Probability of exactly 510 ex-smokers: ",p,"\n"))
```

2. 500 ≤ X ≤ 520

```{r}
x1 <- 500
x2 <- 520
z1 <- (x1 - E_X) / sd_X
z2 <- (x2 - E_X) / sd_X
p <- pnorm(z2) - pnorm(z1)
cat(paste0("Probability of between 500 and 520 ex-smokers: ",p,"\n"))
```

3. 470 ≤ X ≤ 550

```{r}
x1 <- 470
x2 <- 550
z1 <- (x1 - E_X) / sd_X
z2 <- (x2 - E_X) / sd_X
p <- pnorm(z2) - pnorm(z1)
cat(paste0("Probability of between 470 and 550 ex-smokers: ",p,"\n"))
```

### The number of children with a high blood lead level in each of the three situations of Exercise 14, Week 2

> Childhood lead poisoning due to atmospheric pollution is a major public
health concern. Consider the following three situations:
(a) In a group of 100 children, 20 have a high blood lead level.
(b) In a group of 1000 children, 200 have a high blood lead level.
(c) In a certain population, 1 child in 5 has a high blood lead level.

#### Situation (a)

```{r}
# This is a hypergeometric distribution problem.
N <- 100 # total number of children
K <- 20  # number of children with high blood lead level
n <- 10 # number of children sampled
E_X <- n * (K / N)
Var_X <- n * (K / N) * (1 - K / N) * ((N - n) / (N - 1))
sd_X <- sqrt(Var_X)
cat(paste0("Expected number of children with high blood lead level: ",E_X,"\n"))
cat(paste0("Standard deviation: ",sd_X,"\n"))
```

#### Situation (b)

```{r}
# This is a hypergeometric distribution problem.
N <- 1000 # total number of children
K <- 200  # number of children with high blood lead level
n <- 10 # number of children sampled
E_X <- n * (K / N)
Var_X <- n * (K / N) * (1 - K / N) * ((N - n) / (N - 1))
sd_X <- sqrt(Var_X)
cat(paste0("Expected number of children with high blood lead level: ",E_X,"\n"))
cat(paste0("Standard deviation: ",sd_X,"\n"))
```

#### Situation (c)
```{r}
# This is a binomial distribution problem.
n <- 10 # number of children sampled
p <- 1/5 # probability of a child having high blood lead level
E_X <- n * p
Var_X <- n * p * (1 - p)
sd_X <- sqrt(Var_X)
cat(paste0("Expected number of children with high blood lead level: ",E_X,"\n"))
cat(paste0("Standard deviation: ",sd_X,"\n"))
```

# Exercise 3. 
For Exercise 13, Week 2, calculate E X, E Y , Var(X), Var(Y ), E(X - Y ),
and Var(X - Y ). (Hint: How are X and Y connected?)

## Solution

> There are 10 boys and 15 girls in a class. For a survey, 8 students are to
be selected from the class. They are selected at random. Let X denote the number of
boys that are selected, and let Y denote the number of girls that are selected.

We're going to consider this as a hypergeometric distribution problem. 
The total number of students is 25, with 10 boys and 15 girls. 
We are selecting 8 students.

Hypergeometric distribution properties:
$$E(X) = n * (K / N)$$
$$Var(X) = n * (K / N) * (1 - K / N) * ((N - n) / (N - 1))$$

$$
X: N = 25, K = 10, n = 8\\
Y: N = 25, K = 15, n = 8
$$

$$E(X) = 8 * (10 / 25) = 3.2$$
$$\begin{align*}
Var(X) &= 8 * (10 / 25) * (1 - 10 / 25) * ((25 - 8) / (25 - 1))\\
&= 8 * 0.4 * 0.6 * (17 / 24)\\
&= 8 * 0.4 * 0.6 * 0.7083333 = 1.36
\end{align*}$$

$$E(Y) = 8 * (15 / 25) = 4.8$$
$$\begin{align*}
Var(Y) &= 8 * (15 / 25) * (1 - 15 / 25) * ((25 - 8) / (25 - 1))\\
&= 8 * 0.6 * 0.4 * (17 / 24)\\
&= 8 * 0.6 * 0.4 * 0.7083333 = 1.36
\end{align*}$$

$$E(X - Y) = E(X) - E(Y) = 3.2 - 4.8 = -1.6$$

X and Y are connected because the total number of students selected is 8, 
so X + Y = 8. Therefore, 
$$\begin{align*}
X - Y &= X - (8 - X) = 2X - 8\\
Var(X - Y) &= Var(2X - 8)\\
&= 4 * Var(X)\\
&= 4 * 1.36 = 5.44
\end{align*}$$

> NOTE: It might be nice to show this as a curve on a log scale.

```{r}
for (N in 10^(2*(1:4))){
  boys_sample <- rhyper(N, 10, 15, 8)
  girls_sample <- 8 - boys_sample
  E_X <- mean(boys_sample)
  Var_X <- var(boys_sample)
  E_Y <- mean(girls_sample)
  Var_Y <- var(girls_sample)
  E_X_minus_Y <- mean(boys_sample - girls_sample)
  Var_X_minus_Y <- var(boys_sample - girls_sample)
  cat(paste0("N = ", N, "\n"))
  cat(paste0("E(X) = ", E_X, "\n"))
  cat(paste0("Var(X) = ", Var_X, "\n"))
  cat(paste0("E(Y) = ", E_Y, "\n"))
  cat(paste0("Var(Y) = ", Var_Y, "\n"))
  cat(paste0("E(X - Y) = ", E_X_minus_Y, "\n"))
  cat(paste0("Var(X - Y) = ", Var_X_minus_Y, "\n\n"))
}
```

# Exercise 4. 
Suppose that the proportion of defective items in a large lot is p, and suppose
that a random sample of n items is selected from the lot. Let X denote the number of
defective items in the sample, and let Y denote the number of nondefective items in the
sample. Find E(X - Y ) and Var(X - Y ).

## Solution

For a large lot, we can ignore the finite population correction factor and 
treat X and Y as independent binomial random variables.

$$E(X) = n * \frac{n(p)}{n} = np$$

$$E(Y) = n * \frac{n(1-p)}{n} = n(1-p)$$

$$E(X - Y) = E(X) - E(Y) = np - n(1-p) = np - n + np = 2np - n$$


# Exercise 5. 
Let X and Y be independent random variables. Express Var(X + Y ) and
Var(X - Y ) through Var(X) and Var(Y ).

## Solution

The trick here is to use the fact that for independent random variables, 
the covariance is zero...

$$\begin{align*}
Var(X + Y) &= Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2Cov(X, Y) \\
&= Var(X) + Var(Y)
\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}
Var(X - Y) &= Var((1)X + (-1)Y) \\
&= (1)Var(X) + Var((-1)Y) + 2(1)(-1)Cov(X, Y) \\
&= (1)^2 Var(X) + (-1)^2 Var(Y) + 2(1)(-1)(0) \\
&= Var(X) + Var(Y) - 2Cov(X, Y) \\
&= Var(X) + Var(Y)
\end{align*}$$


# Exercise 6. 
Odds in a horse race betting are defined as follows: 3/1 (three to one against)
means a horse is expected to win once for every three times it loses; 3/2 means two wins
out of five races; 4/5 (five to four on) means five wins for every four defeats, etc.

1. Translate the above odds into 'probabilities' of victory.

2. In a certain race in France the odds for the five runners were:
Phillipe Bois 1/1
Gallante Effor 5/2
Satin Noir 11/2
Victoire Antheme 9/1
Comme Rambleur 16/1
Calculate the 'probabilities' and their sum.

3. How much would a bookmaker expect to profit in the long run at such odds if it
is assumed each horse is backed equally? (Hint: assume the true probabilities are
proportional to the 'probabilities' just calculated and consider the payouts corresponding to a notional e1 wager being placed on each horse.)

4. What would the bookmaker's expected profit and its standard deviation have been
if horses had been backed in line with the true probabilities?

## Solution

1. Converting odds to probabilities:

$$3/1: 1/(3+1) = 0.25$$
$$3/2: 2/(3+2) = 0.4$$
$$4/5: 5/(4+5) = 5/9 \approx 0.5556$$

2. Calculating probabilities for the French race:

$$1/1: 1/(1+1) = 0.5$$
$$5/2: 2/(5+2) = 2/7 \approx 0.2857$$
$$11/2: 2/(11+2) = 2/13 \approx 0.1538$$
$$9/1: 1/(9+1) = 0.1$$
$$16/1: 1/(16+1) = 1/17 \approx 0.0588$$

Calculating the sum of the probabilities:

$$0.5 + 0.2857 + 0.1538 + 0.1 + 0.0588 = 1.0983$$

3. To calculate the bookmaker's expected profit, we can assume that each horse is 
backed equally and that the true probabilities are proportional to the calculated 
probabilities. The expected profit can be calculated as follows:

$$\text{Expected Profit} = \sum_{i=1}^{5} (1 - p_i) \cdot \frac{1}{5}$$

where $p_i$ is the probability of the $i$-th horse winning.

$$\text{Expected Profit} = \frac{1}{5} \left( (1 - 0.5) + (1 - 0.2857) + (1 - 0.1538) + (1 - 0.1) + (1 - 0.0588) \right)$$

$$\text{Expected Profit} = \frac{1}{5} \left( 0.5 + 0.7143 + 0.8462 + 0.9 + 0.9412 \right)$$

$$\text{Expected Profit} = \frac{1}{5} \times 3.9017 = 0.7803$$
